Environmental Modelling & Software 19 (2004) 919–928

# Prediction of wastewater treatment plant performance using

## artiﬁcial neural networks

### Maged M. Hamed , Mona G. Khalafallah, Ezzat A. Hassanien

Department of Public Works, Faculty of Engineering, Sanitary and Environmental Engineering Laboratory, Cairo University, Giza 12211, Egypt

Received 6 December 2002; received in revised form 10 July 2003; accepted 15 October 2003

Abstract

Artiﬁcial neural networks (ANN) models were developed to predict the performance of a wastewater treatment plant (WWTP) based on past information. The data used in this work were obtained from a major conventional treatment plant in the Greater Cairo district, Egypt, with an average ﬂow rate of 1 million m3/day. Daily records of biochemical oxygen demand (BOD) and suspended solids (SS) concentrations through various stages of the treatment process over 10 months were obtained from the plant laboratory. Exploratory data analysis was used to detect relationships in the data and evaluate data dependence. Two ANN-based models for prediction of BOD and SS concentrations in plant eﬄuent are presented. The appropriate architecture of the neural network models was determined through several steps of training and testing of the models. The ANN-based models were found to provide an eﬃcient and a robust tool in predicting WWTPperformance.

Keywords: Neural networks; Waste water treatment; Model studies; Prediction; Optimization; Biochemical oxygen demand; Suspended solids

3. Case study

The developed ANN models are applied to El-Gabal El-Asfar WWTP, which is the main WWTP on the east

bank of the river Nile, Egypt, and is considered the lar- gest WWTP in the Middle East. It is being constructed

in three stages to serve an ultimate population of 12 millions. The existing ﬁrst stage receives an average

ﬂow of 1 million m3/day and peak diurnal ﬂow of 1.5 million m3/day. It is expected that the capacity of the

plant will reach 3 million m3/day after completion of the three stages. The plant is of a conventional non- nitrifying activated sludge type and includes screening

To reach the suitable network architecture, several trials for each group have been conducted until the suitable learning rate, number of hidden layers and number of neurons per each hidden layer were reached. The suitable architecture is the one which produced the

minimal error term in both training and testing data.

In this work, a supervised training, backpropagation algorithm is selected. The backpropagation algorithm minimizes the MSE between the observed and the pre- dicted output in the output layer, through two phases. In the forward phase, the external input information signals at the input neurons are propagated forward to

The suitable network architecture for SS prediction, on the other hand, was determined to consist of an input layer with two neurons (for input BOD and SS), a hidden layer with two neurons and an output layer with one neuron (for predicted SS). To reach this ﬁnd- ing, diﬀerent network structure/training rate combina- tions were evaluated. Network structures with one hidden layer containing 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, and 14 neu- rons were evaluated, each for training rates of 0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8, 1, 1.5, 2, 4. This makes the total number of combinations equal to seven structures times 10 learning rates, totaling 70 combinations. A number of training methods were used, including the Fletcher–Reeves conjugate gradient, BFGS quasi- Newton, and the Levenberg–Marquardt algorithms. The latter algorithm proved to be the fastest and most robust. A suitable learning rate was determined to be

1.0 for both models. One hidden layer was proved to be a universal approximator ([Hornik](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [et](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [al.,](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [1989)](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-). Both networks preserve the parsimony principle to improve the generalization capacity of the ANNs. Parsimony principle states that the use of simpler models, with fewer number of parameters, is usually preferable to more complicated ones with more parameters, when- ever feasible ([Lawrence](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [et](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [al.,](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-) [1996)](#sets-for-groups-14-for-bod-and-ss-respectively-r2-delgrange-vn-cabassud-n-cabassud-m-durand-bourlier-l-values-ranged-from-063-to-081-for-bod-and-from-laine-jm-1998-neural-networks-for-prediction-of-ultraﬁltra-).

During the training phase, the MSE ranged from 4.9 to 5.4, and the MSE for the testing phase ranged from

4.1 to 6.1. The mean absolute percent error ranged from around 13% to 17% for all groups. The narrow band of error measures throughout the groups, and for the two modeled parameters (namely, BOD and SS), is an indication of the ANN’s robustness. In essence, the ANN managed to escape being trapped in noise present in the data. The robustness of the ANN models are also shown in the superiority of the ANN with respect to the regression models for all data division groups 1–4 (Figs. 9 and 10).

### 4.3. Model testing

Actual values of BOD and SS in the testing datasets are compared to predicted values by the neural net- work models, to evaluate the models performance. Furthermore, those were compared to the regression- modeled values. Figs. 9 and 10 show these comparisons for groups 1–4, for BOD and SS outputs. Visual inspection indicates that the ANN models resulted in a good ﬁt for the measured BOD and SS data. The quality of match between the ANN-modeled and measured concentrations was determined by regre- ssion analysis.
